faq.q: Why does a cold block my nose?
faq.a: When you have a cold, the lining of your nose swells as the body fights the virus, and it makes extra mucus. Together they narrow the airways so less air reaches the top of the nose.
asks: Why is my nose blocked with a cold?

faq.q: Why is smell such a big part of flavour?
faq.a: Taste buds detect only five basic tastes, but smell can tell apart a huge number of aromas. The brain merges the two, so most of the detail in flavour comes from the nose.
asks: How much of taste is smell?
Do we taste with our nose?

faq.q: How do smells reach my nose when I am eating?
faq.a: As you chew and swallow, aroma molecules travel up the back of the throat into the nose. This route is called retronasal smell, and the brain feels it as part of the taste in your mouth.
asks: How does smell get from my mouth to my nose?

faq.q: Can I still taste anything with a cold?
faq.a: Yes. Your tongue can still sense sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami, and you still feel texture and spiciness. What you lose is the aroma part of flavour.
asks: Is food completely tasteless with a cold?
Can I taste salt with a blocked nose?

faq.q: Does holding your nose change how food tastes?
faq.a: Yes. Hold your nose and eat a jelly bean: you will taste only sweetness. Let go, and the fruit flavour rushes in as aroma reaches your smell cells.
asks: Why does food taste different when I pinch my nose?

facts: Smelling food from inside the mouth, through the back of the throat, is called retronasal smell.
With the nose blocked, people often cannot tell apart foods like apple and raw potato by taste alone.

quiz.say: You pinch your nose and eat a lemon sweet. What will you notice most?
quiz.show: With your nose pinched, a lemon sweet tastes…
quiz.why: Taste buds still sense sweet and sour, but without smell the lemon flavour mostly disappears.

wrong.0: The lemon aroma needs to reach your nose, which is blocked.
wrong.2: Your tongue still works, so sweet and sour remain.
